|quote=In 1971, US president Richard Nixon declared war on drugs, which had become his ''“public enemy number one”''. He was the first US president to allocate substantial funding to [http://www.pbs.org/wgbh/pages/frontline/shows/drugs/buyers/doitwork.html combating addiction and providing treatment]. But these intentions, which so clearly made drugs a priority, may have been less benign than they appeared. An account published [https://harpers.org/archive/2016/04/legalize-it-all/ in the April issue of Harper's], picked up [http://mic.com/articles/138664/the-war-on-drugs-horribly-racist-origins-have-finally-been-revealed?utm_source=policymicTWTR&utm_medium=main&utm_campaign=social#.Ox494vrNQ by Mic], suggests that his real priority was to stigmatise Black people and hippies and legitimise harsh repression against them.

According to John Ehrlichman, a former adviser to Richard Nixon, the White House's rhetoric about the harmfulness of drugs was nothing but a ''“lie”'': a lie designed to target the president's two main enemies at the time directly. These were African American activists, who had just secured victories after years of campaigning for civil rights, and opponents of the Vietnam War, some of whom had become radicalised within the [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_Underground Weather Underground] movement.
|authors=Aude Lorriaux
|article=La guerre contre la drogue de Nixon était un «mensonge» qui visait à casser la communauté noire
